art.text: From around 879 BC the Assyrians developed extremely large schemes of finely detailed narrative low reliefs for their palaces. They were carved in stone or gypsum alabaster and originally painted. The reliefs mostly showed royal affairs, chiefly hunting and war making.

The Ishtar Gate was built in Babylon around 569 BC on the order of King Nebuchadnezzar II. Its walls were finished in glazed bricks, mostly in blue, and the gate stood 15 metres high. It was part of a grand walled processional way leading into the city.

According to one legend, Nebuchadnezzar II built the Hanging Gardens for his Median wife, Queen Amytis, because she missed the green hills and valleys of her homeland. The Babylonian priest Berossus attested to this around 290 BC. The gardens stood beside a grand palace called The Marvel of Mankind.

Ziggurats were huge pyramidal temple towers, first built in Sumerian city-states and later in Babylonian and Assyrian cities. Thirty-two are known at or near Mesopotamia, 28 in Iraq and 4 in Iran. The latest of them date from the 6th century BC.

The Ishtar Gate was the main entrance into Babylon, built in about 575 BC by Nebuchadnezzar II, king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, who exiled the Jews. Its walls carry rows of large relief animals in glazed brick, which is why they have kept their colours. Lions, dragons and bulls are shown, and part of the gate is now reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.

In the Assyrian palace reliefs, animal forms were given predominance, particularly horses and lions. They were represented magnificently and in great detail. The precisely delineated scenes were part of a grand palace art that probably aimed to match the splendour of neighbouring Egypt.

An Assyrian artistic style, distinct from the Babylonian art that was then dominant in Mesopotamia, lasted until the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC. It had emerged well before the Assyrian empire included Sumer.

The Ishtar Gate was decorated with alternating rows of low-relief mušḫuššu (dragons), aurochs (bulls) and lions made of coloured bricks. These animals symbolized the gods Marduk, Adad and Ishtar respectively. The gate was dedicated to the goddess Ishtar.

The Neo-Babylonian period saw a renaissance of culture and artwork. Its kings conducted massive building projects, especially in Babylon itself. They brought back many elements from the previous 2,000 years of Sumero-Akkadian culture.

No surviving Babylonian text mentions the Hanging Gardens, and no definitive archaeological evidence has been found in Babylon. One theory says the legend really refers to a well-documented garden built by the Assyrian King Sennacherib (704–681 BC) at Nineveh, near modern Mosul.

Babylonian temples were massive brick structures whose walls were brilliantly coloured, sometimes plated with zinc or gold as well as tiles. Painted terracotta cones for torches were also embedded in the plaster. Even Assyria, imitating Babylonian architecture, built its palaces and temples of brick although stone was the natural material of its country.

Ancient lists of wonders differed from the traditional seven. The first known list dates to the 2nd–1st century BC. Besides the traditional seven, the Walls of Babylon, the Palace of Cyrus the Great, and the Pergamon Altar appear more than twice across these lists.
art.source_title: Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
tags: Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

art.text: The geographer Strabo (c. 64 BC – 21 AD) stated that the Hanging Gardens were watered by an Archimedes' screw leading from the Euphrates river. He possibly based his description on the lost account of Onesicritus from the 4th century BC.

war.text: The desert city of Hatra withstood repeated sieges by great powers. Roman emperors Trajan and Septimius Severus failed to take it in the 2nd century, and the Sasanian king Ardashir I failed in the 220s. Finally, Shapur I captured its capital in 240/41 and destroyed the city, ending the Kingdom of Hatra.

The Roman–Parthian Wars ran from 54 BC to 217 AD, pitting the Parthian Empire against the Roman Republic and later the Roman Empire. They were the first series of conflicts in what would become 682 years of Roman–Persian Wars.

The Battle of Opis, fought in September 539 BC (the Nabonidus Chronicle dates it to the month of Tashritu), was the last major clash between the Achaemenid and Neo-Babylonian Empires and ended in a decisive Persian victory, possibly a rout. The Persians "took plunder" from the defeated Babylonians, and most translations of the chronicle also speak of a "massacre" of "the people of Akkad", though translators disagree on whether the victims were the population of Opis or the retreating Babylonian army, and W. G. Lambert argues there was no massacre at all. Sippar then surrendered, and Persian forces supposedly entered Babylon without further resistance. Cyrus the Great was proclaimed king of Babylonia.

Around 605 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar II commanded the Babylonian force that met Necho II's Egyptian and Assyrian army at Carchemish, an important crossing of the Euphrates. The battle ended in a major defeat for Egypt and Assyria. The Nebuchadnezzar Chronicle says the Egyptian army was overtaken and defeated in the district of Hamath as it fled, "so that not a single man escaped to his own country", though historians doubt this, since it is unlikely Necho II's whole army was destroyed. The defeat ended Egyptian influence in the Levant and let Babylon expand to the borders of Egypt.

Rome's first incursion against Parthia began in 54 BC and was repulsed, notably at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BC. There Crassus and his son Publius were defeated and killed by a Parthian army under General Surena. Of 42,000 Roman men, about half died, a quarter made it back to Syria, and the remainder became prisoners of war. Later, during the Roman Liberators' civil war, the Parthians supported Brutus and Cassius, invaded Syria and gained territories in the Levant.

In 113 Trajan launched a war on Parthia, conquering Armenia in 114 and northern Mesopotamia by the end of 115. In the last months of 116 he captured Susa and deposed the Parthian king Osroes I, installing his own puppet ruler Parthamaspates. Never again would the Roman Empire advance so far to the east.

Marching north to aid the Assyrians, Necho II met a hostile force at Megiddo led by Josiah, king of Judah, who was allied to the Babylonians. The Judean army was defeated and Josiah was killed in 609 BCE. Necho II then installed Jehoiakim on the Judean throne as an Egyptian vassal.

War over Armenia broke out again in 161, when Vologases IV defeated the Romans there, captured Edessa and ravaged Syria. A Roman counter-attack under Statius Priscus defeated the Parthians in Armenia, and Avidius Cassius invaded Mesopotamia, winning battles at Dura-Europos and Seleucia and sacking Ctesiphon in 165. An epidemic, possibly of smallpox, which was sweeping Parthia then spread to the Roman army, leading to their withdrawal.

In 195, during Septimius Severus's civil war with the usurper Pescennius Niger, rebellions broke out in Mesopotamia and Nisibis was besieged. Severus restored order, then sacked the Parthian capital Ctesiphon. In 198 he re-established a province of Mesopotamia, with Nisibis, elevated to a full colonia, as its capital.

Nisibis and Singara, along with the territory in Adiabene conquered by Diocletian, were lost after the debacle of Julian's Persian expedition in 363. The provincial capital moved to Amida, while the military commander, the dux Mesopotamiae, was based at Constantina.

The Cyrus Cylinder does not mention the Battle of Opis and portrays Cyrus as liberating Babylon peacefully, with the consent of its people. Yet the battle shows that the existing Babylonian regime actively resisted his invasion of Mesopotamia. Pierre Briant describes the victory as followed by "an immense haul of booty and the massacre of those who attempted to resist", and Maria Brosius reads the massacre as a punitive action, "mak[ing] an example of a city trying to resist the Persian army".

Mark Antony sent Ventidius against Labienus, who had invaded Anatolia. Labienus was driven back to Syria, defeated, taken prisoner and then put to death. The Parthians withdrew from Syria after a further defeat near the Syrian Gates, but returned in 38 BC and were decisively defeated by Ventidius, and Pacorus was killed.

After Harran was captured in 609 BCE, the Assyrians fled to Carchemish, where Ashur-Uballit II sought Necho II's aid. The Siege of Harran ended in failure, and Ashur-Uballit II is never mentioned again in any surviving source.

literature.text: Many biblical stories may have been based on earlier Mesopotamian myths. These include the creation myth, the Garden of Eden, the flood myth, the Tower of Babel, figures such as Nimrod and Lilith, and the Book of Esther.

During the Achaemenid period, the Syriac language and Syriac alphabet evolved in Assyria among the Assyrian people. Centuries later they became the vehicle for spreading Syriac Christianity throughout the Near East.

By the 1st millennium BC, Marduk had become a prominent figure in the Enūma Eliš creation myth of Babylonian cosmology. He had around 50 symbolic names, including "king of the gods of heaven and earth" and "creator of mankind". These were statements about his supremacy, not just titles.

The Chaldaean historian Berossus wrote a native history of Mesopotamia, but it did not survive. All that is known of it comes from quotations in Josephus, Ptolemy, Eusebius, Jerome and George Syncellus.

Herodotus' account of Babylon in his Histories is not that of an eyewitness and is not very extensive. He promised a whole section on the history of Assyria, but it was either never written or has been lost.
Ctesias disputed the opinions of Herodotus, but he mistook mythology for history. Greek romance owed to him its Ninus and Semiramis, its Ninyas and Sardanapalus.

Berossus, a Babylonian priest of Marduk writing c. 290 BC, gives the earliest known mention of the Hanging Gardens. Josephus later quoted his description. Berossus is the only source to credit Nebuchadnezzar II with building them.

No extant Babylonian texts mention the Hanging Gardens. One theory holds that they were purely mythical, and that Greek and Roman writers such as Strabo, Diodorus Siculus and Quintus Curtius Rufus described a romantic ideal of an eastern garden.

The Book of Job, written c. 6th century BC, features a disputation between Job and his friends. Assyriologist Samuel Noah Kramer noted that this form is similar to the Sumerian Debate Between Winter and Summer.
Xenophon's Anabasis gives information on the Achaemenid Empire of his time. It is one of the classical accounts that later readers relied on for knowledge of ancient Mesopotamia.

science.text: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were described as a remarkable feat of engineering. They were an ascending series of tiered gardens with many trees, shrubs and vines, resembling a large green mountain built of mud bricks. Hellenic culture listed them among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
tags: Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

science.text: Ziggurats were huge pyramidal temple towers, first built in Sumerian city-states and later developed in Babylonian and Assyrian cities. Unlike many pyramids, their tops were flat. The earliest were raised platforms from the fourth millennium BC, and the latest date from the 6th century BC.

Mesopotamian scribes served as architects, drafting and managing construction for the government, nobility or royalty. Brick was the ordinary building material, and the region's builders developed urban planning, the courtyard house and ziggurats.

There are 32 known ziggurats at or near Mesopotamia, 28 in Iraq and 4 in Iran. Notable ones include the Great Ziggurat of Ur, the Ziggurat of Aqar Quf near Baghdad, and Chogha Zanbil in Khūzestān, the most recent to be discovered.

Babylonian temples were massive structures of crude brick, supported by buttresses, with drains to carry off the rain. One such drain at Ur was made of lead. The use of brick led to the early development of the pilaster and column, and of frescoes and enamelled tiles.

According to one legend, the Hanging Gardens were built by Nebuchadnezzar II for his Median wife, Queen Amytis, because she missed the green hills and valleys of her homeland. They stood beside a palace called The Marvel of Mankind. The priest Berossus attested this around 290 BC.

Assyria imitated Babylonian architecture and built its palaces and temples of brick, even though stone was the natural building material of its country. It faithfully kept the brick platform, which was necessary in the marshy soil of Babylonia but little needed in the north.

politics.text: The Neo-Babylonian Empire was the last polity ruled by monarchs native to ancient Mesopotamia. It began with the coronation of Nabopolassar as King of Babylon in 626 BC. The Achaemenid Persian Empire conquered it in 539 BC, less than a century after the Chaldean dynasty was founded.

Beginning with Adad-nirari II's accession in 911 BCE, the Neo-Assyrian Empire grew into the largest empire in history up to that point. Because of its dominance and an ideology based on world domination, it has been described as the first world empire in history.

In 116 and 117, the Roman emperor Trajan created a short-lived province of Mesopotamia. He captured the city of Susa, deposed the Parthian king Osroes I, and put his own puppet ruler Parthamaspates on the Parthian throne. The Roman Empire never again advanced so far to the east.

In 734 BCE, Tiglath-Pileser led the Assyrian army through the Levant all the way to the Egyptian border. Several states on the way, such as Ammon, Edom, Moab and the Kingdom of Judah, were forced to pay tribute and become Assyrian vassals. In 732 BCE, the Assyrians captured Damascus.

Assyria descended into violent civil wars in 626 BC, which drastically weakened it. In 616 BC the Babylonians, Medes, Persians, Scythians and Cimmerians, former subject peoples of Assyria, allied and attacked the civil war-ridden Assyrians. The Battle of Nineveh in 612 BC left Assyria destroyed for years to come, and the cities fell to sacking and violent destruction: Kalhu (Nimrud)'s buildings were dramatically destroyed in the sacking of 614–612 BC, and many of the bilingual skilled Assyrians died with their language.

Nabonidus left Babylonia to campaign in the Levant. He then settled for ten years in the conquered city of Tayma in northern Arabia, while the crown prince Belshazzar was left to govern Babylonia. Returning around 543 BC, Nabonidus reorganized his court and removed some of its powerful members.

By 540, Cyrus had begun an offensive campaign against the Neo-Babylonian Empire. In late 539, the Persian army won a crucial victory at the Battle of Opis and then triumphantly entered the city of Babylon. Accounts of the night disagree: the Babylonian Chronicles and the Cyrus Cylinder say Babylon was taken "without battle", but Herodotus and Xenophon report a siege, and Xenophon says the Persians killed those they met in the streets and cut down the king's retinue, killing Belshazzar. This ended the reign of the last native dynasty of Mesopotamia.

Babylonia resented Achaemenid rule, as it had resented the Assyrians. At least five rebels proclaimed themselves King of Babylon to restore native rule: Nebuchadnezzar III in 522 BC, Nebuchadnezzar IV in 521–520 BC, Bel-shimanni in 484 BC, Shamash-eriba in 482–481 BC and Nidin-Bel in 336 BC. Ancient sources suggest Shamash-eriba's revolt against Xerxes I had dire consequences for the city. Though no direct evidence exists, Babylon appears to have been severely punished: its fortifications were destroyed and its temples damaged as Xerxes ravaged it.

Jehoiakim died during the three-month siege of Jerusalem and was succeeded by his son Jeconiah at the age of eighteen. When the city fell on 2 Adar (March 16) 597 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar pillaged Jerusalem and its Temple and carried Jeconiah, his court and other prominent citizens, including the prophet Ezekiel, off to Babylon. Zedekiah was appointed king in his place, but the exiles in Babylon continued to consider Jeconiah their Exilarch, or rightful ruler.

Tiglath-Pileser's conquests are noteworthy for their extent and for the large scale of his resettlement policies. He settled tens to hundreds of thousands of foreigners in both the Assyrian heartland and in distant, underdeveloped provinces.

The leader of the coup that deposed Labashi-Marduk was likely the courtier Belshazzar. He proclaimed his father Nabonidus king in Labashi-Marduk's place. The sources suggest Nabonidus was part of the conspiracy but had not expected to become king and was hesitant to accept.
In 260, the Persian shah Shapur I captured the Roman emperor Valerian at Edessa. In the next year, Odaenathus of Palmyra took a stand against Shapur, who eventually retreated.

philosophy.text: Ancient Mesopotamian religion was a consistent and coherent tradition that adapted to the internal needs of its followers over millennia. It was not much changed by the movements of peoples through the region. It is thought to have influenced later Canaanite/Israelite, Aramean and ancient Greek religions.

Babylonian and Assyrian priests read the heavens as the key to their belief system. All gods, demons and spirits had assigned places in the sky, and even political events were interpreted through this astral theology. The system gave birth to astronomy, which was carefully cultivated because knowledge of the heavens was the foundation of the belief.
philosophy.source_title: Religions of the ancient Near East

philosophy.text: In the Iron Age I period, the 12th to 11th centuries BCE, the religion of the Israelites branched out of Canaanite religion as Yahwism. It focused on the worship of Yahweh, whom worshippers conflated with El. Over time Yahwists began denying that other gods existed, and it became more strictly monotheistic.

During the Babylonian captivity of the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, certain circles among the exiled Judeans in Babylon refined existing Yahwist ideas. These included the nature of divine election, law and covenants. Their ideas came to dominate the Jewish community in the following centuries.

From the 5th century BCE until 70 CE, Yahwism evolved into the various theological schools of Second Temple Judaism, alongside Hellenistic Judaism in the diaspora. In this period the text of the Hebrew Bible was redacted into its extant form.
The Bible narrates the discovery of a legal book in the Temple in the seventh century BCE. Most scholars see it as some form of Deuteronomy and regard it as pivotal to the development of scripture.

The Babylonian king Nabonidus favoured the moon god Sîn over Babylon's patron deity Marduk. This religious policy eventually served as a casus belli for Cyrus the Great, who invaded in 539 BC by portraying himself as a champion of Marduk divinely restoring order.

Babylonian and Sumerian ideas of the afterlife show striking parallels with Hebrew belief. The Judaic underworld Sheol is very similar in description to the Sumerian Kur, ruled by the goddess Ereshkigal, as well as the Babylonian underworld Irkalla. Kur was a cold, dark cavern deep beneath the earth where all souls went, whatever their behavior in life, and where the only food was dry dust. Family members poured libations into the grave through a clay pipe so the dead could drink, and under the Third Dynasty of Ur those given poor burials were believed to fare poorly and haunt the living.

In Mesopotamia a new, less tolerant regime took power, imprisoned Mani and executed him as an offender against Zoroastrian orthodoxy. Consistent waves of persecution from Christians, Zoroastrians and Muslims eventually eradicated Manichaeism as a formal religious affiliation within Byzantine and Islamicate realms.

Astral theology divided the ecliptic circle into three zones, a northern, a middle and a southern. Anu was assigned to the first, Enlil to the second, and Ea to the third. The system appears to have been devised by priests, and it absorbed earlier, more popular religious beliefs into one whole.
philosophy.source_title: Religions of the ancient Near East

culture.text: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, described as tiered gardens of trees, shrubs and vines that looked like a large green mountain. One legend says Nebuchadnezzar II built them for his Median wife, Queen Amytis, because she missed the green hills and valleys of her homeland.

Babylonian religion gave its gods moral traits: Shamash, the Sun-God, stood for justice, Marduk was full of mercy and kindness, and Ea was a father-like protector of mankind. Hymns, prayers and elaborate atonement rituals stressed being clean and pure, showing humility, and confessing one's guilt and sins without reserve.
culture.source_title: Religions of the ancient Near East

culture.text: Under the Parthian Empire, Assyria saw a major revival between the 2nd century BC and 4th century AD. Temples were once more dedicated to gods such as Ashur, Sin, Shamash, Hadad, Bel and Ishtar. Christianity was introduced from the 2nd century AD, and Assyria became the centre of the Church of the East.

Cyrus the Great permitted Jews held captive in Babylon to return to Jerusalem and rebuild Solomon's Temple. A number returned in 538 BC, the foundation of the Second Temple was laid in 536 BC, and it was completed in 516 BC, the sixth year of Darius.

The early Persian kings tried to maintain the religious ceremonies of Marduk, the most important god of Babylon. By the reign of Darius III, however, over-taxation and the strain of numerous wars had led to the deterioration of Babylon's main shrines and canals.

By the end of the third century Manichaeism reached the attention of the Roman Empire, which viewed it as a "Persian aberration" with followers who were "despicable deviants". In Mesopotamia, a new, less tolerant regime took over, imprisoned Mani and executed him as an offender against Zoroastrian orthodoxy.

The Babylonian priest Berossus, writing in about 290 BC, attested the legend of the gardens and the palace called The Marvel of Mankind. His description was later quoted by Josephus. The gardens have also been attributed to the legendary queen Semiramis, giving them the alternative name Hanging Gardens of Semiramis.
